claim: Properdin was originally described in 1954 by Pillemer et al. as a serum component that promotes complement activation in an antibody-independent manner.
source: Properdin was originally described in 1954 by Pillemer et al. as a serum component that promotes complement activation in an antibody-independent manner (Pillemer et al., 1954).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pillemer et al., 1954

claim: Properdin binds to and stabilizes the alternative C3 convertase C3bBb, thereby extending its half-life 5- to 10-fold.
source: Properdin binds to and stabilizes the alternative C3 convertase C3bBb, thereby extending its half-life 5- to 10-fold and inhibit its degradation by factor I (Fearon and Austen, 1975; Schreiber et al., 1975; Medicus et al., 1976).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fearon and Austen, 1975; Schreiber et al., 1975; Medicus et al., 1976

claim: Properdin inhibits degradation of C3bBb by factor I.
source: Properdin binds to and stabilizes the alternative C3 convertase C3bBb, thereby extending its half-life 5- to 10-fold and inhibit its degradation by factor I (Fearon and Austen, 1975; Schreiber et al., 1975; Medicus et al., 1976).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fearon and Austen, 1975; Schreiber et al., 1975; Medicus et al., 1976

claim: The role of properdin as a pattern-recognition molecule leading to alternative pathway activation has been disputed since 1958 when Nelson et al. challenged it.
source: However, since challenged in 1958 by Nelson et al., who suggested that the binding of properdin requires the presence of activator-bound C3b, the second conception on the role of properdin as a pattern-recognition molecule (PRM) leading to the alternative pathway (AP) activation has been a matter of dispute (Nelson, 1958; Kemper et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nelson, 1958 and Kemper et al., 2010

claim: Nelson et al. suggested that the binding of properdin requires the presence of activator-bound C3b.
source: However, since challenged in 1958 by Nelson et al., who suggested that the binding of properdin requires the presence of activator-bound C3b, the second conception on the role of properdin as a pattern-recognition molecule (PRM) leading to the alternative pathway (AP) activation has been a matter of dispute (Nelson, 1958; Kemper et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nelson, 1958

claim: Recombinant transmembrane properdin in HEK-293 cells was shown to initiate AP activation.
source: Interest in this concept was renewed when recombinant transmembrane properdin in HEK-293 cells was shown to initiate AP activation (Vuagnat et al., 2000) and surface plasmon resonance methodology confirmed that biosensor chip bound properdin can provide a platform to initiate C3bBbP assembly from purified C3b, factor B and factor D (Hourcade, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vuagnat et al., 2000

claim: Biosensor chip bound properdin can provide a platform to initiate C3bBbP assembly from purified C3b, factor B and factor D.
source: Interest in this concept was renewed when recombinant transmembrane properdin in HEK-293 cells was shown to initiate AP activation (Vuagnat et al., 2000) and surface plasmon resonance methodology confirmed that biosensor chip bound properdin can provide a platform to initiate C3bBbP assembly from purified C3b, factor B and factor D (Hourcade, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hourcade, 2006

claim: Several recent observations have supported the recognition role of properdin in several models of molecular patterns including pathogens, endogenous cells and various biological substrates.
source: In line with those findings, several recent observations have also supported the recognition role of properdin in several models of molecular patterns including pathogens, endogenous cells and various biological substrates (Cortes et al., 2011; Kemper et al., 2008; Xu et al., 2008; Saggu et al., 2013; O'Flynn et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cortes et al., 2011; Kemper et al., 2008; Xu et al., 2008; Saggu et al., 2013; O'Flynn et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2015

claim: Harboe et al. challenged the concept of properdin as a PRM and argued that properdin binding to complement activating surfaces is strictly dependent on initial C3 activation.
source: However, Harboe et al. recently challenged the concept of properdin as a PRM and argued that properdin binding to complement activating surfaces expressing pathogen- and damage-associated molecular patterns, including zymozan, Escherichia coli, Neisseria meningitidis, myeloperoxidase and umbilical vein cells, is strictly dependent on initial C3 activation with subsequent binding of properdin to stabilize C3bBb (Harboe et al., 2012; Harboe et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Harboe et al., 2012; Harboe et al., 2017

claim: Collectin-12 is a newly identified collagen-like molecule with multimeric structure assembled by ~140 kDa subunits.
source: Collectin-12 (CL-12; also known as collectin placenta one or CL-P1) is a newly identified collagen-like molecule with multimeric structure assembled by ~140 kDa subunits and mainly present as a monomer, dimer or trimer (Nakamura et al., 2001; Ohtani et al., 2001; Ma et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nakamura et al., 2001; Ohtani et al., 2001; Ma et al., 2015

claim: CL-12 is mainly present as a monomer, dimer or trimer.
source: Collectin-12 (CL-12; also known as collectin placenta one or CL-P1) is a newly identified collagen-like molecule with multimeric structure assembled by ~140 kDa subunits and mainly present as a monomer, dimer or trimer (Nakamura et al., 2001; Ohtani et al., 2001; Ma et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nakamura et al., 2001; Ohtani et al., 2001; Ma et al., 2015

claim: CL-12 is characterized by an intracytoplasmic domain, a transmembrane domain and an ectodomain subdivided into a coiled-coil domain, a collagen-like domain and a carbohydrate-recognition domain.
source: CL-12 is characterized by an intracytoplasmic domain, a transmembrane domain and an ectodomain subdivided into a coiled-coil domain, a collagen-like domain and a carbohydrate-recognition domain.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about CL-12 structure

claim: The ectodomain of CL-12 is crucial for oligomeric assembly and recognition of various pathogenic or endogenous molecular patterns.

evidence: Supported by citations to Nakamura et al., 2001; Ohtani et al., 2001; Mori et al., 2014

claim: CL-12 was originally defined as scavenger receptor C-type lectin because it shares structural and functional similarities with type A scavenger receptor.
source: CL-12 was originally defined as scavenger receptor C-type lectin because it shares structural and functional similarities with type A scavenger receptor (Nakamura et al., 2001; Ohtani et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nakamura et al., 2001; Ohtani et al., 2001

claim: CL-12 is mainly expressed as transmembrane molecules on cells originating from the endothelium and placenta.

claim: Properdin from NHS was still able to bind CL-12-pre-opsonized fungi in the presence of Cp40, although to a lesser extent than without Cp40.

claim: No binding of properdin was observed in properdin-depleted serum in the absence of Cp40.

claim: After reconstitution with serum properdin, the binding of properdin was comparable to NHS.

claim: Pre-opsonization with CL-12 markedly enhanced the properdin binding in reconstituted serum.

claim: Addition of Cp40 completely removed C3 activation in 100% NHS.

claim: C3 inhibition by Cp40 abolished the Bb deposition in CL-12-opsonized fungi with reconstituted serum.
